summary: We repeat left-to-right passes: in each pass, a neighbouring pair whose difference is at most T is replaced by its average. When a whole pass merges nothing, the sequence is stable (T10 — simulate until stable).

blocks.title: Read N and T from one line
blocks.text: Both values share one line, so we split it. T can be a decimal like `2.0`, so it must be `float` — `int('2.0')` crashes.

blocks.title: Read the sequence as floats
blocks.text: Averages produce decimals, and we print with 2 decimals at the end, so we store floats from the start. (N isn't really needed — the list knows its own length.)

blocks.title: Start a new pass
blocks.text: Each loop of `while True` is one full pass. `new_seq` collects the result, `merged` remembers whether anything changed, and `i` walks the old sequence.

blocks.title: Can this element merge with the next?
blocks.text: We use a `while` with our own index because a merge must skip TWO elements, which a `for` loop can't do. `i + 1 < len(seq)` is checked first so the last element never looks past the end.

blocks.title: Merge the pair
blocks.text: Append the average, jump over both elements with `i += 2`, and note that a merge happened. We compare against the original `seq`, never the new average — the statement continues with the rest of the original numbers.

blocks.title: No merge: keep the element
blocks.text: Copy the element unchanged and move one step.

blocks.title: Finish the pass
blocks.text: The new list becomes the sequence for the next pass. If nothing merged in this pass, nothing will ever merge, so we stop.

blocks.title: Print with 2 decimals
blocks.text: `f"{x:.2f}"` turns `10.5` into `10.50`; `" ".join` puts single spaces between them.

complexity: Each pass is O(N) and each merging pass shrinks the list, so at most N passes: O(N²), about 10⁴ steps for N = 100.
pitfalls: Comparing a fresh average with the next number in the same pass.
